en: Words cannot unfold the reality; speech does not meet the occasion. Those who rely on words perish; those who linger in phrases are deluded.
If it were entirely like this, what connection would there be? One loses the sword in Kunming Lake, yet one finds the saw in the River of the Flowing Spring.

*E-yue e-yue.* For the time being, let us pass through with a rough-and-ready ease. I have recorded this to show the assembly of Zen practitioners, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who have gathered my words.
Winter of the Wuzi year.

Recorded Sayings of Master Gyōkawa, Volume One.
The disciples and incumbent abbot of Luohan Chan Temple on Mount Yanwang, Ben Guang et al., compiled [this record].

On the fifteenth day of the ninth month in the fourth year of the Xianchun era, the Master was invited by Lingyan Chan Temple on Mount Yanwang in Ruian Prefecture to the Chief Seat’s Quarters at Jingci Chan Temple in Lin’an Prefecture; on the twenty-eighth day, he entered the temple.
According to the description of the chamber: "This chamber is deep and vast, inconceivable, like empty space which contains all phenomena;
regarding all objective realms, it makes no discriminations."
Holding up the notice for the hall, he said: "The State Duke, Chief Minister of State: In the past at Vulture Peak, you received the direct entrustment.
All you senior monks, realize this thoroughly and cause the Dharma to abide for a long time."
Pointing to the Dharma seat, he said: "Atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, white waves roll over red dust.
The sages of the three periods, the patriarchs of the six generations, and the old monks of the world—all have no beaks."

Ascending the seat, he held up the incense and said: "This single offering of incense is burned in the precious censer to reverently pray for the longevity of the present Emperor—ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years!
May Your Majesty’s life be as enduring as the mountains and peaks, and may you shine with the brilliance of the sun and moon!"
Next, he picks up the incense and says: "In years past, while traveling on pilgrimage, I arrived at Mount Taibai and encountered the old monk Huangya Du.
He brought up the bamboo shoots of the South Mountain and the cuttlefish of the Eastern Sea; as soon as I was about to open my mouth, I was struck by him.
Thinking back on it today, the pain pierces to the very marrow of my bones—it is not like Linji saying, 'I received sixty blows from my former teacher.'"
It is like a stalk of mugwort used as a brush; I burn it in this precious incense burner as an offering to the Great Monk Tianmu,
the ninth-generation successor of Yangqi, who formerly resided at Tiantong Jingde Chan Temple on Mount Taibai in Qingyuan Prefecture,
in order to repay the kindness of his Dharma-milk.
As he took his seat, a monk stepped forward and asked, "If one wishes to travel a thousand li, the first step is the beginning.
What is this very first step? The Master said, "You have already missed it. The monk said, "Thirty years from now, someone will surely raise this story.
The Master said, "Do not babble so recklessly. The monk said, "I am glad that Yangqi’s true lineage has been transmitted. The Master said, "I told you: do not babble so recklessly."
The assembly prostrated. The Master then gave a shout and said:
"Let the questioning cease for now. The ancients said that both question and answer belong to the realm of gain.
O Zen adepts, how shall you repay the kindness of the King today? Simply recognize my mind: from where does it arise?"

Once you recognize the place of birth, you will recognize its function throughout the twelve periods of the day. Once you recognize its function throughout the twelve periods of the day, you will recognize its function throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Therefore, the appearance of all Buddhas is solely for the purpose of awakening to and clarifying the fundamental mind, taking this as the ultimate goal.
If you can do so, you will naturally complete your task in a single moment; there is no need for further effort.
If one acts for the sake of others, this is merely a conditioned matter; how could it suffice to repay the grace of the unconditioned?
Though the kalpa-stone may wear away, the sovereign’s grace knows no end.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the phrase that is transmitted outside the teachings? The Master said, "It does not fall into the realm of the profound and subtle.
The monk asked, "If so, then one enters directly into the ground of the Tathāgata. The Master said, "Wait; proceed slowly. The monk asked, "What is the place where a student practices?
The Master said, "From where did you just come? The monk asked, "How can one repay the four debts of gratitude and the three [debts]? The Master said, "..."
"There is a way out. The Master said, "Just follow the path you came down a moment ago. [The monk] asked, "What about when a tiger is pressing against the edge of a cliff?
The Master said, "Your life is like a thread hanging by a hair. [The monk] stepped forward and said, "Save me! Save me! The Master picked up his staff and threw it to him.
He then said: "All you sons of the patriarchs, personally clarify your own nature. Do not mistake that which turns toward the fire when cold or seeks the shade when hot for it.
Do not mistake that which remains unmoving for a single thought-moment when earth, water, fire, and wind disperse for it.
Do not mistake this old monk’s opening of his mouth and moving his tongue for it. An ancient said: 'This nature is originally pure and fully endowed [with all virtues].'"
The myriad virtues are merely differentiated according to the two conditions of defilement and purity.

Thus, when the sages awaken to them, they employ them exclusively for purification and thereby achieve the path of enlightenment; when sentient beings are deluded by them, they employ them exclusively for defilement and sink into the cycle of saṃsāra.
Their essence is non-dual. (He strikes his staff once and lets out a shout.)
The night assembly said: "Shaoshi has no gates or doors; how can one immediately attain penetration? The night is cold, so endure standing;

listen as I speak of the East and West. He ascended the hall and said: "With the sword of wisdom, tear asunder the net of outflowing craving. With the vajra hammer, smash to pieces the nest of ignorance."
"The True Person of No-Station is a dry dung-scoop; the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is a broken sand-pot. Even a clear-eyed monk cannot distinguish between them. Entering the hall, he said:
"Each and every one of you, in your own station, who would not be struck by this opportunity? When a Zen guest comes with a question, I, the old monk, go forth to answer. One stroke!"
Forty-nine. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The ancient Buddhas interpenetrate with the pillar; the cat bites the fierce tiger. Suddenly picking up his staff, he said:
"Stepping out the door, one bumps into Subhūti; pressing through the void, the whole body is revealed—a single expanse of empty stillness, beyond all description."
Sentiment: The clear light of ten thousand miles flies upon the jade hare.
Entering the hall: Prajñā is like a great mass of fire; can even a single thread or speck of dust remain? With one punch, the Yellow Crane Tower is toppled;
with one kick, the Parrot Isle is overturned. When there is spirit, add more spirit; where there is no affectation of elegance, there is true elegance.

Windswept Elegance. Ascending the hall: "The green bamboos stand tall; with one strike, Xiangyan forgot all that he knew. The red peach blossoms blaze; with one glance, Lingyun was freed from all doubt.
Chanting praises atop the bell tower, planting vegetables beneath the bed’s feet—Master Sheng, the Head Seat, said: "A fierce tiger!"
Sitting on the road, he gave a shout and said: "If one lacks the strength to lift the cauldron and pull the mountain, a black steed from a thousand li is not easily ridden.

He ascended the hall and said: "A hundred thousand bright mirrors reflect light and shadows upon one another; in every atom and every world-system, each is distinct and does not borrow from the other. Huangbo.
Linji was struck with sixty blows of the staff; Linji then struck Daoyu in the ribs three times with his fist. Heaven is high and earth is deep;
the waters are broad and the mountains are long. Everyone, speak a single phrase before your parents were yet born!
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Intellect, acuity, consciousness, thought, and understanding are the very root of birth and death.
When Guishan asked Yangshan, 'Each and every dharma points upward; speak a single phrase,' how did he respond? As Yangshan was about to open his mouth, Guishan gave a shout."

He asked three times, and Baizhang made three attempts to answer; each time he was met with a shout. Yangshan bowed his head and wept, saying, "Baizhang said, 'I must meet another person before I can attain it.
Today is precisely that meeting. He let out a shout and said, "The very root of birth and death!"
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "The *Madhyamaka-śāstra* says: 'Perfect enlightenment has no name or mark; according with conditions, it is the site of enlightenment.
What is perfect enlightenment having no name or mark? The Master remained silent. The monk asked, "What is according with conditions being the site of enlightenment?
The Master lowered one foot. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "This question is superfluous. The monk stepped forward and said:
"How can you ask such a redundant question? The Master said, "The ancients asked questions as numerous as cow-hairs.
They said that the Buddhas constantly appear in the world to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, never ceasing for a moment.

How is it that not a single sentient being has developed the true resolve to return to the source? To say it is because their craving and attachment are difficult to sever is not correct; it is because their karma is heavy [and thus difficult to overcome]."

"No, it is not so. If the Buddhas did not appear in the world, and did not preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, then sentient beings would naturally give rise to true awakening and return to the source.
This is a gate of remedial teaching (pratipakṣa-dvāra); you must investigate it thoroughly."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "The celestial barrier is shattered; all is vast and open. I, this old monk, walk hand-in-hand with you.
Should someone suddenly ask, 'What is the Buddha?'—it is he who has shattered the celestial barrier."
Ascending the hall, he said: "A single hair swallows the ocean, yet the nature of the ocean remains unimpaired; a tiny speck of dust lands on a sharp blade, yet the blade’s keenness remains unmoved.
Longtan blew out a paper lamp; Deshan fell prostrate in worship. This year, the peach and plum blossoms are precious; each single fruit is worth a thousand pieces of gold."

On the anniversary of the Buddha’s passing, he ascended the hall and said: "When the mind within the three realms is exhausted, this is nirvana. Mountain flowers are red as brocade; stream water is deep blue as indigo.
He ascended the hall again and said: "In the Great Sui dynasty, while burning a clearing, I saw a snake. I prodded it with my staff toward the fire and shouted: 'This one!'"
Even the physical form has not yet been relinquished; you shall die right here. It is like obtaining a lamp in the darkness.
Abiding in the world as if in empty space, like a lotus flower unsullied by water, the mind is pure and transcends that [world].

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Before the world was formed, there were no names for Buddhas and no names for sentient beings. As soon as the world was established, there arose these many designations.
Although there are many such designations, they are merely provisional names; from the beginning, they possess no substantial reality.
Do not mistake them for something real. There is nothing to do—take care."

A small *chán* (meditation) discourse on New Year’s Eve. A monk stepped forth from the assembly and said, "If Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land and the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven," the Master replied, "To whom would Zhang Gong sell his straw sandals? The monk then withdrew.
The Master then said: "The First Patriarch said, 'Mind upon mind is like wood or stone. The Second Patriarch said, 'Utterly forgetting all conditions.
Caoxi said, 'Do not deliberate on good or evil at all. These are ordinary words, yet how many people sit within their verbal tracks?
He can do nothing for you; he only requires that you investigate the mind. This mind has been unborn from the very beginning, nor will it ever cease."
Extinction. Neither arising nor ceasing. It is like wood or stone; naturally forgetting all conditions, what existence can there be for good or evil?
Mañjuśrī said: "The mind is like empty space; empty space leaves no trace. The sun and moon merely revolve in their cycles. He further said:
"This very moment is the night of the thirtieth day of the twelfth month."
Ascending the hall: Meeting face-to-face, no brow is raised; you go east, and I go west. Desiring to call out to one another upon meeting, we are speechless, our gazes fixed.
This is all the mere breath of rice and gruel. Adhering closely, without a single seam or crack—how many such people can there be?
In the city of Wenzhou, they are as numerous as the sands.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The entire earth is shivering with cold; throughout the ten directions, it is a tumultuous uproar.
He held up his staff and said, "I let pass the Baguā Monk, yet I pierce through the nostrils of Xiakōng."
Ascending the hall on the Buddha’s Birthday: Before Mount Huayin lies a well a hundred feet deep; within it flows a cold spring that pierces the bones.
Whose daughter comes here to view her reflection? She does not look at anything else, but gazes upon the side of her neck. Thus was Prince Siddhārtha born.
For the sake of the Abbot Heng’s entry into the stupa: A three-legged donkey trots on its hooves; it tramples through the Great City of Nirvana, where green grass grows from within the skulls.
Entering the hall, he said: "When Deshan saw a monk enter the gate, he would drag out his staff and strike him immediately. When Muzhou saw a monk enter the gate, he would..."
It is said: "Seeing this established case, I grant you thirty blows. This is not because I wish for him to attain Buddhahood on level ground;
it is simply because he must let go completely. Nowadays, the monastic communities are thin and desolate because everyone is unwilling to relinquish their attachments.
O assembly, where do you place that which you see before you? Where do you place that which is stored within your breast? Let it go! Let it go!
Where does attachment reside?
To extinguish the fire for the temple master, you have come as the temple master. Do you understand? The Buddha in the hall is one who has realized the truth;
from between his brows, he emits the white tuft of light, shattering the skulls of all sentient beings throughout the great earth. A torch!
Nor is there any place of attachment.
On the anniversary of the late Master Tiandong’s passing, Tianmu offered incense and said: "Baling did not prepare a vegetarian feast for Yunmen in gratitude;
he relied solely upon three turning words. Today, at Lingyan, we do not prepare a feast for the anniversary of our late teacher, the Venerable Tiandong; nor do we have those three [turning words]."
A turning word. Do you all understand thoroughly? When our former teacher was alive, he could not be moved by any of his disciples' wiles in his presence.
Since it is so when born, it is likewise so after death.
He performed the funeral rites for the practitioner Lu. Looking at the assembly, he said, "This was Practitioner Lu. After the cremation, he retrieved the stone girdle that had fallen from his waist.

He then ascended the hall and said: "The earth element is great; the water element is great; the fire element is great; the wind element is great. If for a single thought-moment there is no doubt, the earth cannot obstruct you.
If for a single thought-moment there is no craving, the water cannot drown you. If for a single thought-moment there is no anger, the fire cannot burn you. If for a single thought-moment..."
There is no joy; the wind cannot blow it away. Such a person is one who follows the Way without reliance. The Buddha is born from non-reliance;
if one awakens to non-reliance, even Buddhahood is not attained.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "All dharmas are without marks, yet whatever meets the eye takes form. Prajñā is without cognition, yet it reflects in response to conditions.
I show this directly to you; if you do not understand, the direct path becomes circuitous."
Opening the furnace, he ascended the hall and said: "Xuefeng said, 'The Buddhas of the three periods of time turn the Great Dharma Wheel within the flames.
Yunmen said, 'The flames preach the Dharma for the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and the Buddhas of the three periods of time stand upon the ground and listen.
O assembly, which is more intimate: that which the Buddhas turn, or that which the flames preach? If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander them."
The Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma.
Ascending the hall, he shifted the void so that not a single speck of dust could stand. Suddenly picking up his staff, he said, "Do you all see Lingyan’s staff?
After a long pause, he said, "I thought the monkeys were white; it turns out there are also black ones."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The waters of the sea do not freeze.
He then said, "The single, firm, and dense body manifests within all atoms of dust.

Suddenly picking up his staff and holding it crosswise, he said, "Han Xin facing the court—the ten directions of the world are empty and desolate; the ocean of three thousand lands is cold and still."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all, without exception, this single adamantine eye.

It is also oneself. Those who are masters of universal penetration shall together bear witness to it. The Great Way has no front or back; the ultimate principle transcends words and explanations. It stands far beyond the Three Vehicles."

Transcending the ten stages, descending from his seat, ascending the hall, and sitting in meditative repose within the crags, heavenly flowers rained down—this too was like flies swarming toward putrid meat. At Shaolin, he sat facing the wall.

Severing one's arm to find peace of mind is somewhat like burning paper money to summon ghosts; even if one were to break free from the old masters' molds, they would still strike three thousand blows in the morning and eight hundred blows in the evening.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Deshan said: 'There is no birth-and-death to be feared; there is no nirvana to be attained; there is no bodhi to be realized.
It is simply an ordinary person of no affairs. To speak thus is to give rise to affairs. Once affairs arise, how can one not fear birth-and-death?
Since one fears birth-and-death, there is then a nirvana to be attained and a bodhi to be realized. Brothers, all..."
[The Master] said: "Words cannot be gathered.
He ascended the hall, held up his staff, and said: "The ocean of nature is boundless. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are its waves; the sun, moon, and stars are its waves.
The Buddhas of the three periods have their nostrils soaked through. If you all wish to emerge from this, you must proceed with caution."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "There was once a question posed to Zhaozhou: 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature?

Zhaozhou replied, 'No. What is the meaning of this? The Master let out a great laugh. The monk asked, "Master, I do not understand why you laughed. The Master said, "I laugh because you, a lacquer bucket, are not yet clever enough.
The monk asked again: "It is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; why then [did Zhaozhou say no] regarding the dog?"
“Do they not have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, “Because they still possess the consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*).
[The monk asked,] “Is this truly definitive? The Master said, “What is not definitive about it? [Another] asked, “Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said, “It has.
[The monk asked,] “Master Zhaozhou is seven hundred years old; why does he have two tongues? The Master said, “An old man is naturally like this.”
Question: "Furthermore, why did you enter this skin-bag? The Master said: "Knowing it yet deliberately committing it. He requested: "Please, Preceptor, clarify this for me.
The Master said: "How much have I darkened [your understanding]?"
He then said: "When Niaoke blew on his robe-hair, the attendant attained awakening. Holding up his staff, he said: "Clouds break apart beyond the heavens;
a snake startles within the grass. He addressed the assembly:
"This matter requires only that each person awaken for themselves. The Buddhas of the three periods have no dharma to transmit or receive. The six patriarchs..."
The Patriarchs have no dharma to transmit; the old monks of the world have no dharma to transmit. A monk asked Linji, "Whose song do you sing, Master?
Whose ancestral style do you succeed? Linji said, "At Huangbo’s place, I asked three times and was struck three times.
As the monk hesitated, Linji gave a shout and followed it with a blow, saying, "One must not point toward emptiness."
"In the midst of emptiness, he drives in a stake. "How can one drive a stake into empty space?

Furthermore, a presiding master asked, "Are not the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings not for the purpose of clarifying Buddha-nature? Linji said, "The overgrown weeds have never been cleared away.
The master said, "Would the Buddha ever deceive people? Linji said, "Where is the Buddha? The master was speechless. Linji—
He said, "In the presence of the Attendant, you intended to deceive this old monk. Retreat quickly! Retreat quickly! Look at him acting like this—what transmission or reception could there be?
There is nothing to be awakened to either. From immeasurable kalpas until today, it has been thus.
Judging by the portion belonging to each of you, there is not even a hair’s breadth of deficiency in any of you. You have finished eating your congee; go wash your bowls. At times, he would also say:
Whether speaking a single phrase for oneself or addressing others, there is in total no distinction between the real and the unreal. I, this old monk, shall now utter a phrase:
it would shatter Mount Sumeru into fine dust, draw the waters of the four great oceans into a single pore, turn one meaning into infinite meanings, and turn infinite meanings into one meaning.
A fragrant breeze comes from the south, and the halls and pavilions give rise to a subtle coolness.
"Cool! Sentient beings are inverted; deluded about themselves, they pursue external objects. If one can master these objects, one is identical to the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. These words require no searching."
Simply observe that the five aggregates are all empty and the four elements are without self; realize this directly and instantaneously.
The "True Person of No Station" is starkly bare, yet he hides his body within the Big Dipper. Among the multitude, people often treat this as a Zen convention, but let me ask you:
what is Zen? It is not that which is momentarily luminous and empty; it is not that which is silent and still; it is not that which one investigates; nor is it awakening.
This is not it. The tiny ant can settle anywhere, yet it alone cannot settle upon a flame.
Sentient beings can take objects as conditions, yet they alone cannot take Prajñā as an object. With a single stroke of the brush, it is struck down.
When the practitioner at Stone Chamber stepped on the pestle and forgot to move his foot, where did he go?
Ascending the hall, he said: "The physical body is the form; the Dharma-body is the nature. All good and evil arise entirely from the Dharma-body, not from the physical body.
If the Dharma-body commits evil, the physical body will not be born in a favorable realm; if the Dharma-body performs good, the physical body will not fall into an evil state.
Ordinary people see only the physical body and do not see the Dharma-body; thus they are unable to practice the giving that is free from abiding in signs."
Giving. One who cannot practice impartial conduct in all places and cannot universally respect all sentient beings is not one who sees the Dharma-body.
One who sees the Dharma-body is able to practice giving without abiding in signs, is able to universally respect all sentient beings, and is able to cultivate the practice of Prajñāpāramitā.
This is the true characteristic. For the sake of you all, [I have] set this aside...
The four great elements and the five aggregates come forth to meet this old monk and perform the cremation for the Venerable Ayi.
This Dharma-seal of mine is preached for the sake of benefiting the world;
thus, fire issues from all eighty-four thousand pores, utterly consuming the seeds of Bodhi and withering the grove of merit.
Ascending the hall, he said, "Old Teacher Wang teaches you to act among those of different species. He clenched his fist with his hand, placed it on his head, and said, "Is this a donkey or a horse?
Bring a bundle of straw tomorrow!"
The Abbot was about to extinguish the fire for the deceased senior monk when Xuansha said, "Before the face of a deceased monk is precisely Bodhi before one's eyes.
Raising a torch, he said, "The kalpa-fire blazes fiercely; the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, yet only Bodhi is indestructible."
Ascending the hall, a monk stepped forward and asked, "For half a year, I have been under the Master’s seat contemplating the story of the cypress tree, yet I find no point of entry.
Today, I hope the Master will show me compassion and provide a skillful instruction.
The Master shouted, "Do you intend to come here to peddle your wares? The monk bowed. The Master said, "Who would believe you?"

He then said: "O Great Assembly! Even if you were to overturn the great ocean, kick over Mount Sumeru, scatter the white clouds with a shout, and shatter empty space, you would still not have made even half a true monk.
This tradition of my school is vast and expansive; its majestic power is sovereign and free."
Therefore, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the butcher Wide-Face cast down his butcher’s knife and said, "I am counted among the thousand Buddhas.

Within the Great Assembly, the powerful Mara King waited until all sentient beings had attained Buddhahood and the realm of sentient beings was emptied, only then giving rise to the Bodhi-mind. True lion cubs; excellent lion roars!
Ascending the hall, he called to the assembly, saying: "Form and sound are the lethal poison of non-arising; sensation and perception are the pitfall of the ultimate person.
He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an example: Once, while Baizhang was walking with Mazu, they suddenly saw a wild duck fly past.
Mazu asked, "What is that? Baizhang said, "A wild duck. Mazu asked, "Where has it gone? Baizhang said, "It flew away.
Mazu then seized Baizhang by the nose; in the throes of pain, Baizhang cried out, "Ai-ya! Ai-ya! Mazu said, "And you say it flew away?"
"Indeed! It has always been right here. At these words, the Master was so overcome that sweat poured down his back.
Having attained realization through this, he returned to the attendants' quarters and wept bitterly. A fellow practitioner asked him, "Have your parents passed away?
The Master replied, "No. The fellow asked, "Have you been insulted by someone? The Master replied, "No. The fellow asked, "Then why are you crying? The Master replied, "My nose!"
The Master gripped him so painfully that his companion said, "What karmic connection was not in accord?
Baizhang replied, "You should ask the Master yourself. The companion then went to ask Mazu, who said, "He understands it himself; you should ask him.
When the companion returned to the quarters, Baizhang laughed heartily. The companion asked, "Just now you were weeping; why are you laughing now?"

[Baizhang] laughed. Mazu said, "Just now you were weeping; now you are laughing. The next day, when Mazu ascended the hall and the assembly had just gathered, Baizhang went out and rolled up the sitting mats.
Mazu immediately descended from his seat and returned to the abbot’s quarters, where he called for Baizhang and asked, "When I ascended the hall just now, I had not yet preached the Dharma.
Why did you roll up the mats? Baizhang replied, "Yesterday, Master..."
One day, Mazu grabbed Baizhang by the nose until his head ached. Mazu asked, "Where were you paying attention yesterday?
Baizhang replied, "Today my nose does not ache anymore. Mazu said, "You understand the matter of today thoroughly.
Baizhang then bowed and withdrew. Later, while attending Mazu again, as Baizhang stood in attendance, Mazu looked at the whisk in the corner of the meditation seat.
The Patriarch said, "Is it this very function? Is it apart from this function? Mazu took up the whisk and held it upright.
The Patriarch said, "Is it this very function? Is it apart from this function? Mazu hung the whisk back in its original place.
The Patriarch let out a thunderous shout. Mazu said, "It was enough to deafen my ears for three days."
The Master said: "His nose was pinched; he lost his voice from the pain. What does that have to do with the wild ducks flying away?
One moment crying, the next moment laughing—this is the outburst of a mad nature. Mazu said, "It is he who understands. Why not use the fodder appropriate to your own station?
He then ascended the hall, rolled up the sitting mat, and said, "Yesterday my nose was pinched by the Master until it hurt; today I am turning [the matter over]."
"There is no connection. Mazu asked, "Where did you focus your attention yesterday? He replied, "Today my nose does not ache either.
Mazu said, "You know the matter of today very well. This was one question and one answer.
He visited Mazu again. Placing head upon head, he let out a shout and then descended from his seat.
During the summer retreat, he gave a small discourse: "The ten directions gather together; chirping and twittering, each one studies non-action.

Toiling and bustling, this is the field for selecting Buddhas. *Du!* When the mind is empty, one returns having passed the imperial examination. Since the mind is already empty, what further is there?
"Return! Layman Pang’s words were like a dream; this old monk’s words are likewise like a dream. If this dream is shattered, not a single dharma remains.
When not a single dharma remains, the myriad dharmas burst forth in clarity. A fragrant breeze blows from the south; the halls and pavilions grow cool. An iron boat floats upon the water.
*Hah!* A blind turtle and a lame tortoise drift aimlessly through the void, needlessly causing the fisherman to hold his hook.

Ascending the hall, he raised an example: Once, while Baizhang was working together with the community to hoe the earth, he suddenly saw a monk who, upon hearing the drum roll, lifted his hoe and laughed loudly before simply returning to his quarters.
Baizhang remarked, "How brilliant! This is the gateway through which Avalokiteśvara enters into principle.
Upon returning, Baizhang called for the monk and asked, "Just now, what principle did you perceive that you acted in such a manner? The monk replied, "I heard—"
[The Master] said, "The sound of the drum. Go back and eat your meal. The Elder simply smiled. The Master said, "This is precisely the gateway through which Avalokiteśvara enters into principle.
One day, seeing his brothers citing ancient and modern precedents, he asked them, "Regarding your own portion [of realization], what do you have?"

In the course of their discussion, the monk was speechless. The Master struck him with a staff and said, "To cite the ancients and to cite the present—this is you. To be unable to open your mouth—this is you.
On the Dragon Boat Festival, he ascended the hall. Longya said, "One who studies the Way must first have a cause for awakening; it is like once having competed in a race against a swift dragon."
"Boat! Although it is an old pavilion and an empty field, once you have won it back, only then will there be rest. He took up his staff, threw it down, and returned directly to the abbot’s quarters.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is 'hearing again causes the cataracts of the sense-organ to be removed'? The Master said, "One is not; two is not.
The monk asked, "What is 'when the dust is cleared away, awareness is perfectly pure'? The Master said, "A leaking wooden ladle; a broken colander."
It is said: "A wooden woman pierces a needle as the mountain colors grow exquisite; a stone man pulls a thread as the sea clouds arise.
Master Gaomao, with his bare feet red, strides straight up to the crown of Vairocana."
Ascending the hall: No dharma exists before one’s eyes; every dharma is distinct and resonant. Outside the mind there is no stimulus; every stimulus corresponds perfectly.

The Buddha of the Sun’s Face, the Buddha of the Moon’s Face—what are the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns? A single wild goose in the autumn stars; a thousand households with their mortars and pestles at night.

At the opening of the assembly at Xiébǐngfúzhāi, the Master ascended the hall and said: "The wheel of food turns, and the wheel of Dharma turns; this old monk joins his palms and receives it upon his head.
As the Sūtra says: 'He who gives to you is not called a field of merit; he who makes offerings to you will fall into the three evil realms.'"

I am performing the cremation for the Vice Abbot Cong. Throughout your life, you were clever and possessed sharp intelligence; though you could calculate by the thousands and tens of thousands, at this point, none of it is of any use.
You should simply let go of body and mind; do not wait until you are adding straw to the flames.
Ascending the hall, he said: "A mighty warrior extends his arm without borrowing another's strength; one who skillfully wields the Great A-sword does not injure his own hand.
Holding up his staff, he said: "Transversely spanning the universe, a single phrase settles the fundamental principle."
Ascending the hall, he said: "If there were even a single dharma, Vairocana would fall into the state of an ordinary person and never again return for kalpas on end.
If there were not even the ten thousand dharmas, Samantabhadra would lose his realm and have nowhere to go."
The donor ascends the hall. Everywhere, he stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high; vividly, his constant radiance manifests before him. As it says in the scriptures:
"In the first watch of the day, the middle watch of the day, and the final watch of the day, he gives away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: When Baizhang ascended the hall, Yunyan Cheng came forward and asked, "Master, for whom do you labor so busily every day?
Baizhang said, "There is one person who wants it. Cheng said, "Why do you not let him make it himself? Baizhang said, "He has no household goods.
The Master [Zhaozhou] said: "Where is that person who wants it? Although he has no household goods, why not let him make it himself?"
[He] finally attained [enlightenment]. Ascending the hall, he said: "There are no three realms from which to escape; this is the sentient being. There is no bodhi to be sought; this is the Buddha.
Buddhas and sentient beings are neither one nor two. Therefore it is said: 'In nature and characteristics they are equal; bodhi, liberation, and karma [are likewise so].'"

[He] obstructed the afflictions. Ascending the hall, he said: "Cold and heat have overgrown the weeds in the field of the mind; the sword of wisdom is a thing of no use. He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Last night the earth shook and the reed-ash rose; at the tip of every blade of grass is an inch of spring. Shake up your spirit!
Hurry and take it up! Birth, old age, sickness, and death do not spare anyone.

On the first day of the month, he ascended the hall. Master Yunmen said: "The entire universe and great earth, being without even a hair’s breadth of fault or affliction—this is still a 'turning phrase.
Not seeing a single form is but half the teaching. You must know that there is a further time for the 'full presentation.'"
The Master held up his staff and said: "This staff turns the Great Dharma Wheel above your heads, all you people.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time turn the Great Dharma Wheel beneath your feet, all you people. Thus do all sentient beings realize Equal and Perfect Enlightenment."

The Venerable Yanqing performed the cremation ceremony. "Formation, Abiding, Destruction, and Emptiness. "Formation" refers to this single body of one's own, which is a provisional combination of the four great elements.
"Abiding" refers to sitting upon a curved wooden chair. "Destruction" refers to the separation of the four great elements, such that the body no longer exists.
"Emptiness" refers to the fact that light and darkness, form and emptiness, are without the slightest obstruction or impediment. Raising the torch, he said: "Fire!"

The nature is fundamentally empty; formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness do not abandon or separate from one another. All things are thus. To see through to the root source is like planting flowers upon a rock.
[Ascending the hall,] he raised his mallet and held up his whisk—scarifying healthy flesh to create sores. To cite the present and cite the past is to wet one's bed while wide awake. Even if...
There is a separate vital spark; it is also a public proclamation. It is not like this at all: an unperforated iron hammer.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Evil is a sinful karma; good is also a sinful karma. When sinful karma is eliminated, it is a clear blue sky and a bright sun.
Xihe plays with lions; Fenggan rides a fierce tiger. Old Xuansha sets up his signboard; Master Deng beats a clay drum."
Ascending the hall for the Summer Retreat: Before the fifteenth day, I shall not ask; after the fifteenth day, there will be no leisure to ask.
Right now, on the fifteenth day itself, bring forth a single phrase! Even if you could speak it, it would still be but half a phrase.

Protecting life and observing the summer retreat—the decree is strict in the Western Heaven. Since the Buddha entered nirvana, two thousand two hundred and twenty years have passed. There has been none...
To those who do not comply, he strikes once with his staff and immediately descends from the seat.
Entering the hall, he says: "Entering the mundane and entering the sacred; entering the defiled and entering the pure; entering the true and entering the conventional.
Why is this so? A lotus flower grows from the mud. He then recites a verse: A lotus flower grows from the mud, Its natural form is uniquely distinct; Emerging from the water, yet not emerging.
At that time, he fed the fish and the turtles;
because he suspected the vice-abbot of having set fire to the estate, he supervised the monks who were milling the rice, his head and face covered entirely in dust.
Returning, he leaps into the fire to bathe; he emerges with the pure body of Vairocana.
Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked: "When Zhaozhou was asked, 'What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? he replied, 'The cypress tree in front of the hall.'"
There was one who asked Qingyun, "In the courtyard before you, there is no cypress tree. Both were questions regarding the meaning of the Westward Journey;
why then did their answers differ? The Master said, "It is not that you, O brother, have asked it; even this old monk does not know."
It is said: "At the bottom of the great ocean, no corpses remain; within the Tathāgatagarbha, not a single dharma abides.
Carrying my staff slung across my shoulder, I heed no one as I go straight into the thousands and tens of thousands of peaks."
He performed the cremation for the Head Seat Yu. Yu took the fire and tested it, saying:

"If this were the jade of He Pu or the suspended Li, the Chui Ji or the Jie Lu—their substance would become ever more lustrous and their color ever more pure through a thousand smeltings and ten thousand refinements. It is like Yunmen, who was pressed by Muzhou until his single leg was broken;
he was ten parts closer to death. [Yunmen] threw down the torch and said, 'Indeed! Yu likewise threw down the torch and said, "Indeed!"
Ascending the hall: The five thousand and forty-eight fascicles are but yellow leaves used to stop a child’s crying. If you were a man of true caliber, you would turn away upon being touched by them.
To serve as the general head seat for the cremation ceremony: there are countless dead men on level ground; he who can penetrate the thorn-brake forest is the one.
"Excellent! Today, one must not say that the head monk in the hall has no superior qualities.
He raised the firebrand and said: "Siri siri."
At the opening of the assembly at Xiébǐngfúzhāi, he ascended the hall and said: "The offering of food satisfies one so completely that one forgets a hundred hungers;
the offering of Dharma causes the flowers of the mind to blossom forth, illuminating the lands of the ten directions. This may be called a merit not bestowed in vain. He raised his staff and said:
"The rat has been caught; the oil jar is broken."
For the sake of the Sangha, we perform the communal labor (*pǔqǐng*) and descend to the fire. You all, each possesses a single point of wondrously luminous true nature.

Even when the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the world is utterly destroyed, this nature is not destroyed. Whether reading sutras, sitting in meditation, folding up one’s bedding, spreading out one’s bowl, performing communal labor for the benefit of others, passing through birth and death, or moving and acting—everything is entirely this nature. It is only because of a single moment of delusion.
Delusion! You turn your back on awakening and unite with the sensory dust, unaware of where you have fallen. I have now pierced this through for you. Step back, step back!
A fire-serpent comes to pierce your skull. [He] throws down the torch.

Ascending the hall, he raised this case: When Zen Master Linji arrived at Longguang, as Longguang was ascending the hall, Linji stepped forward and asked, "Without deploying any sharp blades, how does one achieve victory?
Longguang remained seated. Linji said, "Great Teacher of Virtue, do you have no skillful means?"
Longguang stared with wide-open eyes. Linji pointed his finger and said, "This old fellow has met his defeat today. The Master said:
"Today, everyone in the assembly says that Linji asked [the question] without deploying a single sharp edge;
how could he have achieved victory? Longguang sat there holding his ground. How tragic! When masters meet, why must it depend on words and forms? Even someone three thousand *li* away can know this."
“This dull-witted fellow!
[The Master] addressed the assembly: “Brothers in the hall, come to the Abbot’s quarters and request that I burn incense and preach a general discourse.

Looking up, I see your sincere desire to establish and flourish this monastic community. However, this matter does not reside in words. Throughout his entire life, Bimiashramana did nothing but hold up his staff.”
Throughout his entire life, Master Zhizhi did nothing but point his finger; throughout his entire life, Master Dashi did nothing but strike the ground.
Though they split Mount Tai and Mount Hua asunder and tore the Yellow River apart, they could not yet connect with even one or half of one person.

If I were to speak of it, heavenly flowers would fall in profusion, rendering further words unnecessary. You in this assembly are each and every one great men; throughout the twelve hours of the day, there is no [other way].
Not even a hair’s breadth of leakage. Amidst the heaps of red dust, one is hurriedly tossed about; within the shadows of the green mountains, one drifts aimlessly.
This is precisely the moment when a butcher lays down his cleaver and becomes a Buddha on the spot. Yet, you must not understand it in such a way.
If you understand it in such a way, you fall into the category of intellectual understanding; you will be bound by that understanding and wander about in confusion.
Not a single step can be taken. Brightness is obstructed by brightness; darkness is obstructed by darkness; form is obstructed by form;
emptiness is obstructed by emptiness; and speech is obstructed by speech. This is why one sinks into the ocean of suffering of birth and death, with no possibility of emerging.

When the ancients were firm and stable beneath their heels, they were naturally radiant and unimpeded in every direction; they would take up a dead snake and immediately know how to handle it with life.
Have you not seen it? A monk asked Mazu, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Mazu called to him to come forward.
When the monk had come forward, Mazu struck him and said, "Six ears do not share a secret. Master Huanglong Nan said:
The ancients valued the Way. Six ears do not share the same counsel, let alone three hundred or five hundred people deliberating in a vast clamor—calamity, calamity!
As for those who rely on intellectual understanding, how can they ever grasp it? Even if you were to calculate until Maitreya descends to be born, there would be no place for you to find a foothold.
Only when intellectual understanding is forgotten and all clever stratagems are exhausted is it like viewing the myriad phenomena in a clear mirror, down to the finest hair.
There is no concealment. Since there are no obstructions anywhere, one may point to a deer as a horse or take south for north; letting go and gathering back, every step is free.
Only then can one come forth to extend a hand, not blinding the eyes of practitioners.

When the venerable master Songyuan was nearing his death, he offered this final instruction: "Among those who have long studied and walk the true path, there are none who cannot employ the 'black bean' method."
It is difficult to shoulder the true lineage; the Buddha-dharma of Linji has sunk low to this point. How painful, how painful!

The words of our late master contain a profound meaning. Those who seek to walk the authentic path are like picking out the moon from among the stars—how much more so for those who employ the "black bean" method?
Brothers, if you are a man capable of a single stroke that severs both parts, what does the black bean method matter?
It is difficult to apply. Master Zhimen said, "Black beans are good for making sauce; this very thing is it.
In recent years, the monastic communities have become desolate and uninspiring. This is because those who occupy the curved wooden seats are all merely followers of intellectual understanding.
They argue over which koan is a means of saving others and which is not, delighting only in superficiality.
To play with words alone is called "the upward-facing core. To fear that others will speak of mind or nature is called "the principle of the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, there is a certain class who specialize in creating novel phrases and call this "transcending the norm," thereby luring in those newly entering the assembly.
If it were like this, how could our school have reached the present day? Observe De Shan, Lin Ji, and the two regions of Zhao and Mu.
What kind of standard do the various elders of Yunmen possess? Is there a head and face that you can see? Is there a place for you to settle and dwell?
Beneath a thousand ages, they shine forth as clearly as the sun and moon suspended in the sky. The Sixth Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying:
"I have an object that has no head and no tail, no name and no character, no back and no face. Do you all recognize it? At that time, there was...
Hozō Shinkō came forth and said, "This is the original source of all Buddhas; it is the Buddha-nature of Shinkō.
The Sixth Patriarch struck him with a staff and said, "You talkative śrāmaṇera! Even what I call 'a thing' does not suffice, let alone this 'original source' and 'Buddha-nature.
In the future, even if this fellow covers his head with a mere thatch roof, he will only become a follower of the school of intellectual understanding."
Tudu said, "The Dharma-eye of the ancients was never mistaken in its predictions. To establish intellectual understanding as the core principle today is precisely what Heze did.
If one practices Chan without such insight, one merely dwells in the house of the Yellow-Faced Old Man and eats the food of the Yellow-Faced Old Man;
yet this is not even equal to a young man from a village of three households who, brother to brother, cultivates his own field. He then withdrew.

Step back. Turn toward the base of your heels and silently apply yourself to this. Possessing such an eye and such a mind, you have completely pierced through the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Yet, the Buddha has still not let you go. Within my school, it is like the water of the great ocean;
the deeper one enters, the deeper it becomes. You must reach the very bottom before you can succeed. But how does one reach the bottom? Simply discern.
With a sincere heart, I shall certainly not deceive you. Take care.
[The Master] ascends the hall for the *zhai* (feast) following the incense-bearer’s service and says: "To provide food as an offering to all of you is a good intention;
to provide the Dharma as an offering to all of you is a good intention. With three copper coins, one marries a dark old woman who does not comb her hair nor wash her face."
Knowing whether he was ordinary or holy, [the Master] gave a shout.
He ascended the hall and said: "There is one phrase. I shall present it to you all; each of you, gather your thoughts and listen.
This one phrase is the phrase from before the parents were yet born. The ancients did not call it 'one phrase'; had they called it 'one phrase,' it would have become dead."
Therefore, do not investigate the "dead word," but investigate only the "living word": "When you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it;
carry it home in a bottomless basket."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The small dung pit, the great dung pit—come forth, you who cannot be drowned!
I have a phrase to tell you: 'What is the Buddha? A dried-up dung pellet."
Ascending the hall for the Summer Retreat: This old monk, all of you, the Buddhas, and all sentient beings—sentient and insentient alike—are all things within a cloth bag.
Who is there to tie the mouth of this cloth bag shut?
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: Once, when the Seat-Holder Huo came to visit Baizhang, they drank tea together.
Afterward, Baizhang said, "I have a matter; may I ask you about it? Huo replied, "Fortunately, this is not a matter of words; why must you obstruct me?

Baizhang said, "If that is so, then I permit your inquiry. Huo said, "Please give me another cup of tea. Baizhang said, "Having secured Annam, you still worry about the north of the Great Wall. Huo—[remained silent].
Huo pried open his chest and said, "In this way, in this way. Baizhang said, "Nevertheless, it is difficult to grasp; nevertheless, it is difficult to grasp. Huo said, "If you know, you will get it;
if you know, you will get it. The Master said: "They met as equals, yet among them there was a subtle excellence.

When the Venerable Huo pried open his chest and said, 'In this way, in this way,' Baizhang remarked, 'Nevertheless, it is difficult to grasp; nevertheless, it is difficult to grasp. Old [Baizhang]..."
The Saṃgha can lift him up, but they cannot grasp him. Entering the hall, he said:
"All dharmas, from the very beginning, have always been of the nature of quiescent extinction. The spring grasses are lush and green; the summer trees are dense and dark."
The autumn wind whistles; winter ice breaks into flakes. Holding up his staff, he said: "All of you, from morning until evening, you run up and down.
*Recorded Sayings of Guangli Chan Temple on Mount Aśoka in Mingzhou*
On the twenty-sixth day of the third month in the twentieth year of the Zhizhi era,
the General Superintendent dispatched a monk-envoy from Yanjing, carrying an official decree, to the Fangu Liáo (Pastoral Office) at Mount Yandang in Wenzhou.
A Request for the Master to Serve as Abbot of Guangli Chan Temple on Mount Aśoka in Mingzhou.
Formerly the Abbot of Donghu Xiashu, Daoguan, composed the "Petition for the Master from the Rivers and Lakes" (Jianghu qingshu), which says:
The Mo-ling mountains to the east are the Vulture Peak of the Eastern Continent; the Mo-ling mountains to the west are the Vulture Peak of the Western Heaven.
When the True Body Stupa emerges, it is as if the Buddha has appeared before us, subduing the mountains and rivers so that the noble land and its people may correspond to one another.
At the Eastern Hall of Nengren, Zen Master Hengchuan continued the lineage of Linji, Yangqi, and Ying’an. His preaching was devoid of artificial refinement or ornate embellishment;
his words were suited to the times and truly served as a vajra-king’s precious mallet for shattering the mountains of demonic delusions.
Although the capital city of Yanjing and Yandang Mountain were separated by several thousand li, [the influence reached there].
The general summons and the specific invitation were issued to exclude all others, for such was the reverence shown to his Way.

Although he should have remained in seclusion to grow old, he responded to the needs of the age at an opportune time, mindful that the ancestral path must not be abandoned or sink into ruin; thus he came to serve as a stabilizing pillar in the midst of the stream.
On the second day of the eighth month, the Master entered the temple.
At the Buddha Hall, he burned incense and said: "The thirty-two marks cause devas and humans to look up in reverence; the eighty minor marks cause ghosts and spirits to tremble with awe."
Ascending the seat, he held up the incense and said:

"This one offering of incense is to pray for the longevity of the present Emperor—ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years! Next, holding up the incense again, he said:
'On behalf of the Crown Prince, may his years of life reach a thousand autumns; may the rank and emolument of all the court officials be further increased.'"
Next, holding up the incense, he said:
"I offer this for the sake of the National Preceptor, the Great Master, and the Grand Director of the Sangha, to increase their years of Dharma.

He then took his seat. As a monk stepped forward from the assembly intending to ask a question, the Master gestured with his hand to have him withdraw, saying: "Venerable Elder, wait; listen to this old monk."
The Disposition (Chufen) states: "Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the Buddha-dharma is manifest. Yet, therein lies the cause of delusion regarding the sense bases and their objects.
Therefore, the Great Master Bodhidharma said: 'I have come to this land to preach the Dharma and save those lost in delusion. One flower opens into five petals.'"
The result is spontaneously accomplished. Now, to provide support is precisely to accord with sudden enlightenment. When the eye sees form, it is not obstructed by form;
when the ear hears sound, it is not obstructed by sound. As for all the sense faculties, none are obstructed. The imperial wind forms a single expanse.
"The Sun of Wisdom remains perpetually bright.

[The Master] ascends the hall and says: "O Venerable Elders! To realize one's own mind and understand one's own mind is to dwell in the Pure Land without joy and to abide in an evil world without resentment.
But how does one realize it? How does one understand it? Some say: 'A large month has thirty days; a small month has twenty-nine.'"

Twenty-nine. If it is thus, then various phenomena arise. Where there is arising, there is cessation. Since arising and ceasing do not stop, how can one attain thorough penetration? You must be extremely careful.

Ascending the hall, he said: "What is there to say about whether the Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear? What is there to say about whether the Patriarch came from the West or did not come from the West?
To single-mindedly uphold [these questions] is a great affliction; to expound upon them is a great affliction; to maintain that it is none of these things is also a great affliction."
Ascending the hall: Eyes fixed upon the clouds and sky, standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high; with heads covered in ash and faces smeared with dust, trailing mud and water.
When the wild jackal howls, it is the lion’s roar; when the lion roars, it is the wild jackal howling. Thirty years hence, there will be one who attains realization.
A Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat: In all antiquity, there has never been such a hall of dragons and elephants. Their solemn countenances, as pure as ice and frost, illuminate the four quarters.

In this arena where the Buddha is chosen, there is nothing to choose; in the passing of the mind through emptiness, one attains the degree and yet has nowhere to return. This old monk need not strike his seat or brandish his whisk.
Nor should one speak of East and West; the ladle-handle of the Western house is short, while that of the Eastern house is long. There is no need for everyone to deliberate over it:
"What kind of vegetables are we eating today? Two years share the same spring. To take up the phrase: how would you say it?
On the twelfth day of the fourth month in the twenty-first year of the Zhiyuan era,

I reverently received the Imperial Edict appointing me as the abbot of this temple. Having led the assembly in burning incense and gazing toward the palace to express our gratitude for the imperial favor, the ceremony concluded.
Ascending the seat, he said: "The Yellow River clears once every three thousand years; a Sage appears once every five hundred generations.
The majestic High God governs the Golden Wheel: to the east it reaches Yuyi, to the west it extends to Meigu, and to the south it reaches Jiaozhi."
To the north lies Youdu; the six armies and the myriad commoners all receive its majestic spiritual power.

It is just as the śarīra-relics and precious radiance of Śākyamuni Tathāgata illuminate the four continents. In the ancient Mount Mao of Qingyuan Prefecture, I have twice received imperial edicts, receiving exceptional favor and grace.
Thus, this field of rubble was transformed into a palace of the Yama and Tuṣita heavens, bringing about this for me, a poor monk.

They have entered the realm of rest and liberation. Imperial grace fans far and wide; the precious calendar is ever renewed. Auspiciousness is welcomed within the Crane Prohibited Gates (*hejin*), and those in the ranks of the *yuán* (the imperial court) sing of his virtue.
Holding up his staff, he said: "The void may be measured and the wind may be bound, yet none can fully describe the Buddha’s merit."
A Minor Sermon for the Summer Retreat. Three time-limits are established to urge the snake to transform into a dragon; the waxen man serves as the test.

The patriarchs of the Western Heaven—whether protecting life or taking it—involve themselves with both extremes. To deliberate on these two paths is a double error; it is merely to exhaust one's breath and labor like hoeing a patch of fallow field.
One sows a basketful of millet; the toil is no small matter. Eating but one meal at midday and sleeping but once after nightfall—this does not exceed the bounds of ordinary sentiment.
Yet the monks within the King Aśoka Monastery are each and every one detested by others. If you have a staff, I give you a staff;
if you have no staff, I snatch your staff away from you.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Ordinary people and sages differ, yet their nature is no different. When the weather is hot, the path of ordinary people is hot; one cannot say that the path of the sage is not hot.
When the weather is cold, the path of ordinary people is cold; one cannot say that the path of the sage is not cold. Throughout the earth and under heaven it is thus.
It simply requires seeing one's nature. Seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood. A Buddha is precisely an ordinary person; an ordinary person is precisely a Buddha."
The Buddha ascended the hall. A monk asked, "The fundamental nature is pure and still; why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
The Master said, "Why have you made this one question?"
It is said: "Striking open the gate of great liberation; consciousness grasps that which has no face. Fully releasing and fully gathering; fully killing and fully reviving.
The ten directions of the world are a single mass of iron; white hairs grow upon the back of empty space."
Addressing the assembly: In my school, there is not a single dharma to give to others. Bodhidharma’s coming from the West was merely to provide witness.

Each and every one is fundamentally complete from the beginning. From immeasurable kalpas until this very day—whether moving about, bowing, responding to circumstances, interacting with things, relieving oneself, or passing through birth and death—not a single hair’s breadth is lacking, nor is there a single hair’s breadth in excess. This is simply the Great Master himself.
Perform three prostrations and stand in your assigned place. To succeed to the ancestral seat is as people do today:

they claim to possess Chan and the Way, yet they carry their bags and alms bowls, wandering east, west, south, and north in search of it. When emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed; when conceptualization changes, the essence becomes alienated.
Furthermore, they encounter a certain class of false teachers who point east and mark west, only increasing their delusions. Simply let this heart of wandering and seeking come to rest.
The fundamental realm manifests spontaneously; how can it be brought to rest? If you wish to bring it to rest, you cannot.

Throughout the twelve periods of the day—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—all of these are your places of rest. When Yajñadatta lost his head, he sought a place for his mind to rest, but found no such thing.
A Buddha is one who has nothing to do. Long ago, when I was first traveling as a monk, I also believed this.
There was a monk who, three times by day and three times by night, held up the word "Wu" (No), examining it from every angle—horizontally and vertically. He could not penetrate it;

his mind remained wide open like a red-hot iron ball, with no rational way to comprehend it. Eventually, he arrived at the assembly of the former Master. One day, he entered the room for private instruction.
Take up the *gū* bamboo shoots of the Southern Mountains and the cuttlefish of the Eastern Sea; as soon as you open your mouth, you are struck. At that very moment, everything is vast and clear:
the single word "Mu" is shattered into a hundred fragments. What Buddhas are there? What self is there? What myriad dharmas are there?
This is precisely the primordial state, the field of ease and peace. Master Yushan had a wandering monk arrive at his [hermitage].
At the place where he was staying, he asked another, "How do you practice Chan? The monk replied, "Just look at how one advances from the top of a hundred-foot pole.

The Master said: "This illusion is itself the true nature. Good and evil both emerge from within this true nature.
He cited Vipaśyin Buddha, who said: "One borrows the four great elements to form a body; the mind is originally without birth, arising only because of objects."
"If the external object does not exist, the mind also does not exist. Sin and merit arise like illusions and likewise perish.

Quoting the Buddha Krakucchanda: "To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body; to realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-illusion.
When one realizes that the nature of both body and mind is empty, how does such a person differ from the Buddha?"
The Master said: "The Buddha-body is neither real nor unreal; the Buddha’s illusion is not an illusion. He cited the Buddha Kanakamuni, saying:
"If the Buddha does not perceive a body, he knows himself to be the Buddha. If there were a real knowing, there would be no other Buddha.
The wise are able to know that the nature of transgression is empty; they remain composed and are not terrified by birth and death."
The Master said: "The nature of sin is fundamentally empty;

birth and death circulate in a cycle. He then cited Kāśyapa Buddha, who said: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure and clear; from the beginning, there has been no birth and nothing that can be extinguished.
This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit."
The Master said: "A precept-breaking bhikṣu does not enter hell.
He then raised up Śākyamuni Buddha and said: "The Dharma is fundamentally no-dharma; no-dharma is also dharma.

The Master said: "I bow my head in homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.

Śakra raised his hand. The Venerable One said, "So it is, so it is."
The Master said: "All of you understand it at the point where Śakra raised his hand; but how do you understand it before he has raised his hand?

Dwelling within the realm of delusive thoughts, one does not apply clear understanding; because of this lack of understanding, one fails to discern reality.
